common_name: Tiger Tooth Jujube (Deeply Serrated-Leaf Elongated Sweet-Tart Jujube)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; Tiger Tooth is named for its unusually deep, tooth-like leaf serrations, distinct from the smoother-edged leaves of most jujube cultivars, and bears elongated, sweet-tart fruit ripening August-September.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than nearly any other fruit tree once established, making them outstanding low-input choices for Gulf South heat. Tiger Tooth takes its name from its distinctively deep, sharply pointed leaf serrations, a visually unmistakable trait among jujube cultivars, and produces 2- to 3-inch elongated fruit with a crisp, apple-like texture and sweet-tart flavor when harvested at the tan, semi-dry stage in late summer to early fall. It bears within its first two to three years and, like other jujubes, shrugs off the heat, humidity, and periodic drought of a Gulf Coast summer with little complaint. Prune only lightly to remove crossing or damaged branches, and expect vigorous root suckering, which can be mowed or dug and transplanted to propagate new trees.

common_name: Russian #2 Jujube (Black Sea, Earliest-Ripening Compact Jujube)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; Russian #2, also sold as Black Sea, is a compact jujube selection noted for ripening its small teardrop-shaped fruit earlier, by July, than nearly any other jujube cultivar.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than nearly any other fruit tree once established. Russian #2, also known as Black Sea, is a compact-growing jujube cultivar prized for producing the earliest-ripening fruit of any commonly grown jujube selection, with small, sweet, teardrop-shaped fruit ready to harvest by midsummer, well ahead of later-season cultivars, extending the jujube harvest window when planted alongside them. Its smaller mature size also makes it a practical choice for tighter home garden spacing. As with other jujubes, it thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South and needs minimal care once established. Prune only lightly, and manage root suckers, which can be left to form a thicket or removed to keep a single-trunk form.

common_name: Sihong Jujube (Dense Crisp Caramel-Flavored Fresh-Eating Jujube)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; Sihong is a widely acclaimed Chinese jujube cultivar rated by American growers among the best-tasting available, with dense, crisp, caramel-flavored flesh, ripening September.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than nearly any other fruit tree once established. Sihong is one of the most highly regarded jujube cultivars grown in the United States, consistently rated by fruit collectors and evaluation trials among the best-tasting available, prized for its dense, exceptionally crisp texture and rich, caramel-like sweetness that develops fully as the fruit ripens to a mahogany-brown color in September. It bears within its first few years and, like other jujubes, tolerates Gulf South heat, humidity, and periodic drought with minimal input once established. Harvest at the fully colored, slightly wrinkled stage for peak sweetness, and expect vigorous root suckering, which can be managed by mowing or used to propagate additional trees.

common_name: Deer Magnet American Persimmon (Heavy Annual Fruit-Drop Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding root disturbance to the long taproot; Deer Magnet was selected specifically for exceptionally heavy, reliable annual fruit drop, valued for both eating and wildlife food plots.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding root disturbance to the long taproot native persimmons develop early in life. Deer Magnet is a named American persimmon selection prized above all for the sheer volume and reliability of its annual fruit drop, a trait that made it a favorite among wildlife food-plot growers before its excellent eating qualities also drew fresh-eating enthusiasts, producing abundant deep-orange, soft, honey-sweet fruit through fall once fully ripened. Like other native persimmons, the fruit is harshly astringent while firm and must be allowed to soften fully, or be picked up once it drops, before eating. The tree develops a deep taproot and tolerates heat, drought, and marginal soils far better than typical orchard fruit trees once established, and as a native species it is right at home in the Gulf South's heat and humidity. Plant a second, genetically distinct persimmon cultivar nearby for pollination and heavier fruit set.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
wildlife food plot nursery variety notes

common_name: Nikitskaya Bordovaya Hybrid Persimmon (Self-Fertile Crimean Custard-Flavored Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Nikitskaya Bordovaya is a self-fertile Crimean-bred hybrid between Asian and American persimmon, producing large deep-red, non-astringent-when-ripe fruit with a custard-like, peach-toned flavor.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, average soil in full sun. Nikitskaya Bordovaya is a Crimean-bred hybrid persimmon, crossing Asian kaki persimmon back onto the American species (in the lineage of the well-known Rosseyanka), combining the American parent's cold hardiness and vigor with fruit quality closer to Asian persimmon: large, deep red-orange fruit with a rich, custard-smooth texture and a distinctive honeyed, peach-like flavor once fully soft-ripe. It is self-fertile, setting a reliable crop without a second tree nearby, though yields can improve with a pollinator present, and it shows good adaptability across a wide hardiness range, performing well in both the humid Gulf South and considerably colder climates. Fruit ripens in October and, like other hybrid and American persimmons, should be allowed to soften fully before eating to avoid astringency. An easy, low-input tree once established, tolerating heat, drought, and a range of soils.

common_name: Sweet-Ark Immaculate Blackberry (Late-Ripening Firm Thornless University of Arkansas Release)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tissue-culture transplants in late winter or early spring; Immaculate is a 2023 University of Arkansas release, thornless, bred for late-season ripening after most other blackberry cultivars have finished, with unusually good post-harvest firmness.

directions: Plant rooted canes or tissue-culture transplants in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; prune floricanes to the ground after harvest to maintain plant vigor. Immaculate, marketed as Sweet-Ark Immaculate, is one of the newest releases (2023) from the University of Arkansas blackberry breeding program that also produced Apache, Arapaho, Navaho, Kiowa, and Ouachita, distinguished by its notably late ripening window, extending the fresh blackberry harvest well past when earlier Arkansas cultivars have finished, and by exceptional post-harvest firmness that holds up unusually well in storage and shipping compared to older, softer varieties. The thornless, self-supporting canes make harvest easy and scratch-free. As with other Arkansas program releases, it has proven well suited to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South growing season. Water consistently during fruit development for the best size and flavor.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — blackberry variety releases

common_name: UFGlo Peach (Low-Chill White Non-Melting-Flesh Florida Peach)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; UFGlo, bred at the University of Florida for subtropical winters, needs fewer than 150 chill hours and bears white, non-melting flesh, ripening around May.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; because UFGlo needs so few chill hours, it is one of the few peach cultivars reliable in the immediate Gulf Coast and Florida climate where winters may not deliver enough cold for standard peach varieties to bloom and fruit properly. Bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville, UFGlo requires fewer than 150 chill hours below 45°F, allowing it to break dormancy and bloom reliably even after mild subtropical winters, then ripens by early May, well ahead of most Southern-adapted peaches. The white flesh is firm and non-melting, holding its texture well for fresh eating, canning, or short transport, with a mild, sweet flavor. As with other very-low-chill peaches, expect a shorter productive lifespan and somewhat smaller fruit than higher-chill Northern cultivars, and maintain a preventive fungicide program, since brown rot and bacterial spot pressure is high in humid Gulf Coast summers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Stone Fruit Breeding Program
University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences
specialty low-chill fruit nursery variety notes

common_name: UFGem Peach (Low-Chill Yellow Clingstone Florida Peach)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; UFGem, bred at the University of Florida for subtropical winters, bears firm yellow clingstone, non-melting flesh, ripening around May and suited to central-to-south Gulf Coast plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. UFGem, bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville alongside UFGlo and other low-chill selections, requires only a small number of chill hours, allowing it to break dormancy and bloom reliably even after a mild Gulf Coast or Florida winter. It bears firm, yellow, non-melting clingstone flesh with good sweetness and mild acidity, ripening in early May and holding up well for fresh eating or short-distance transport. As with other very-low-chill peaches, expect a somewhat shorter productive tree life and smaller fruit size than higher-chill Northern cultivars, and maintain a preventive fungicide program for brown rot and bacterial spot, both of which are aggressive in humid Gulf Coast summers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Stone Fruit Breeding Program
University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences
specialty low-chill fruit nursery variety notes

common_name: UFRoyal Nectarine (Vivid Red-Skinned Very Low-Chill Nectarine)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; UFRoyal, bred at the University of Florida, needs only about 250 chill hours and bears near-100%-red-skinned fruit over firm, non-melting yellow flesh, ripening roughly 85 days from bloom in early May.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. UFRoyal, bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville for the subtropical Deep South, needs only about 250 chill hours to break dormancy reliably, making it well suited to zone 8b-10 winters too mild for most standard nectarines. Its skin colors an especially striking, nearly solid deep red over firm, non-melting yellow flesh, giving it strong fresh-market eye appeal, and the fruit ripens quickly, roughly 85 days from bloom, in early May. As with other nectarines, it is more susceptible to brown rot than fuzzy-skinned peaches in humid Gulf Coast conditions, so maintain a preventive fungicide program through fruit development and ripening. Expect a somewhat shorter productive tree life than higher-chill Northern cultivars, typical of very-low-chill stone fruit breeding.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Stone Fruit Breeding Program
University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences
specialty low-chill fruit nursery variety notes

common_name: AU-Homeside Plum (Disease-Resistant Auburn University Gulf South Plum)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; AU-Homeside is an Auburn University plum release bred with strong resistance to bacterial spot, canker, and leaf scald, the diseases that most trouble plums under Gulf South humidity, ripening mid-summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and plant a second, compatible plum cultivar nearby for pollination and reliable fruit set. AU-Homeside, part of Auburn University's plum breeding program alongside AU-Rosa, AU-Amber, AU-Producer, and AU-Cherry, was developed specifically for strong resistance to bacterial spot, bacterial canker, and leaf scald, the trio of fungal and bacterial diseases that most limit plum production under the humid, disease-favoring conditions of the Deep South. It bears a solid mid-summer crop of flavorful fruit on a tree that requires substantially less fungicide input than susceptible standard plum cultivars to stay productive and healthy. As with the rest of the AU series, it is well matched to Gulf South heat, humidity, and disease pressure, making it a lower-maintenance choice for home orchards in the region. Prune to an open center for good air circulation, which further reduces disease pressure.
sources: Auburn University College of Agriculture — Stone Fruit Breeding Program

common_name: Peach Chinese Chestnut (Fuzzy Peach-Skin-Textured Reliable Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Peach is a modern Ohio-bred Chinese chestnut selection named for its faintly fuzzy, peach-skin-textured shell, needing a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Peach, a modern selection from Ohio's Empire Chestnut Company, takes its name from the faintly soft, fuzzy texture of its shell surface, reminiscent of a peach skin, a distinctive tactile trait among Chinese chestnut cultivars, and is valued as a reliable, consistent annual producer of good-flavored nuts. Like other Chinese chestnut selections, it carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that eliminated American chestnut from Eastern forests, and begins bearing meaningful crops within a few years of planting. Nuts drop free of the spiny burr at maturity in late September to mid-October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely for the broad mature canopy and good air circulation, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

common_name: Kuling Chinese Chestnut (Historic Early USDA Introduction, Dunstan Parent Stock)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Kuling is one of the original early-1900s USDA Chinese chestnut introductions, later used as founding parent stock for the Dunstan hybrid chestnut breeding line.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Kuling holds a special place in American chestnut breeding history as one of the original Chinese chestnut selections introduced by the USDA in the early twentieth century in the search for blight-resistant chestnuts to replace the vanishing American chestnut, and its genetics were later used as founding parent stock in developing the widely planted Dunstan hybrid chestnut line. It carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight and produces medium-sized, sweet, reliably annual nut crops, dropping free of the spiny burr in October for easy collection. Space trees widely for their broad mature canopy and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range for best nut set.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

common_name: Meiling Chinese Chestnut (Historic Large-Nut USDA Introduction)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Meiling is a historic early USDA Chinese chestnut introduction, sister selection to Kuling, valued for large, sweet nuts.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Meiling is a sister selection to Kuling among the early twentieth-century USDA Chinese chestnut introductions that helped establish blight-resistant chestnut breeding in America, valued for producing unusually large, sweet nuts of good eating quality on a tree that carries the strong natural blight resistance characteristic of Chinese chestnut. It bears reliably within a few years of planting, with nuts dropping free of the spiny burr at maturity in October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely to accommodate their broad mature canopy and the air circulation that helps limit fungal disease pressure in humid summers, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

common_name: AU Gobbler II Chinese Chestnut (Early Extended-Drop Auburn University Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU Gobbler II was selected by Auburn University for early, extended nut drop beginning in early September and continuing four to five weeks, a companion to the earlier AU Gobbler I.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Gobbler II, developed through Auburn University's chestnut breeding program specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the Deep South, was selected for its early and unusually extended nut drop, beginning around the first week of September and continuing over four to five weeks, spreading the harvest window and the wildlife forage value well beyond that of single-flush cultivars, and complements the related earlier-released AU Gobbler I. Its smaller nuts (roughly 5.7 grams) are typical of trees bred with wildlife food-plot use in mind, though it is equally suited to home orchard planting for its reliable annual bearing and blight resistance. Space trees widely for their broad mature canopy and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range.
sources: Auburn University College of Agriculture — Chestnut Breeding Program
Chestnut Growers of America variety notes
wildlife food plot nursery variety notes

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Lipan is a 2011 USDA-ARS release (Cheyenne x Pawnee) bred at Brownwood, Texas for excellent scab resistance and regular, non-alternate annual bearing, nuts maturing about two weeks after Pawnee.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun; Lipan is a Type II pollen shedder, so pair with a Type I cultivar such as Cape Fear or Pawnee for reliable cross-pollination. Released in 2011 by the USDA-ARS pecan breeding program at Brownwood, Texas from a Cheyenne x Pawnee cross, Lipan was specifically selected for excellent resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that most limits pecan production in humid climates, combined with regular, non-alternate annual bearing that avoids the boom-and-bust cycles common in older cultivars. Nuts mature roughly two weeks after Pawnee, extending the harvest window when the two are planted together, and the tree comes into bearing relatively young for a pecan. Supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and harvest once the shucks split open in fall.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Pecan Breeding Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Nacono is a USDA release (Cheyenne x Sioux) with unusually elongated, banana-cluster-shaped nuts and bright straw-colored kernels, harvest around early October.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun, and plant a compatible Type I pollinator such as Cape Fear or Pawnee nearby, since pecans require cross-pollination from a genetically distinct cultivar for best nut set. Nacono, a USDA release from a Cheyenne x Sioux cross, is visually distinctive among pecan cultivars for its unusually elongated nut clusters, which hang in long, curved, banana-like bunches rather than the more rounded clusters typical of most cultivars, containing nuts with bright, attractive straw-colored kernels and good flavor. Harvest occurs around early October once the shucks split open. Supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and provide the deep, loose, well-drained soil pecans need for healthy taproot development.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Pecan Breeding Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection

common_name: Ellis Pecan (Consistent Annual-Bearing Georgia Heritage Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ellis is a Georgia chance-seedling selection valued for very consistent annual bearing, medium scab resistance, and heat/drought tolerance comparable to Cape Fear and Sumner, harvest in October.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun, and plant a compatible pollinator cultivar of the opposite pollen type nearby. Ellis is a chance-seedling selection out of Georgia that has earned a lasting place among Southern pecan growers for its unusually consistent annual bearing, avoiding the alternate-bearing boom-and-bust cycle that troubles many pecan cultivars, along with medium resistance to pecan scab and heat and drought tolerance comparable to well-regarded Gulf South standards like Cape Fear and Sumner. Medium-sized nuts of good flavor and kernel percentage mature and drop free of the shuck around October. Supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and provide the deep, loose, well-drained soil pecans need for healthy taproot development.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pecans
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection

common_name: Floriana Muscadine Grape (Self-Fertile Pierce's-Disease-Resistant Red Wine Muscadine)

planting.note: Plant rooted vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun; Floriana, bred by Florida A&M University, is a self-fertile red-fruited muscadine developed specifically for Pierce's-disease-resistant red wine production, ripening August-September.

directions: Plant self-fertile vines in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy two-wire trellis, since muscadines are vigorous, long-lived vines that need substantial permanent support. Floriana, bred by Florida A&M University, was developed specifically to fill a gap in muscadine wine production: while most muscadine wine cultivars produce white or bronze fruit, Floriana bears deep red berries suited to producing genuine red muscadine wine, combined with strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that devastates traditional bunch grapes across the Gulf South and much of Florida. Being self-fertile, a single vine sets a full crop without a pollinator. Fruit ripens in August and September. Prune annually in winter to renewal spurs along the permanent cordons to maintain productivity and vine health.
sources: Florida A&M University College of Agriculture — Muscadine Breeding Program

common_name: Florida Onyx Muscadine Grape (Large-Cluster Black Fresh-Market Muscadine)

planting.note: Plant rooted vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun; Florida Onyx, a Florida A&M fresh-market release, bears unusually large, deep black-red berries in dense 8-15-berry clusters with extended shelf life, ripening August-September.

directions: Plant vines in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy two-wire trellis, since muscadines are vigorous, long-lived vines that need substantial permanent support. Florida Onyx, released by Florida A&M University's muscadine breeding program for the fresh market, is notable for forming unusually dense, tight clusters of 8 to 15 large, deep black-red berries, far more than the loose groups of three to five berries typical of most muscadine cultivars, giving it a bunch-grape-like cluster appearance while retaining the thick skin, disease resistance, and heat tolerance of true muscadine. The berries also hold their quality unusually well after harvest, extending shelf life for fresh sales or home storage. It shows good resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that limits bunch grape production across the Gulf South. Prune annually in winter to renewal spurs along the permanent cordons to maintain productivity.
sources: Florida A&M University College of Agriculture — Muscadine Breeding Program
